catalog_quote: Syllables with long vowels (indicated in the data with a double vowel) and diphthongs are considered to be heavy and always attract stress (except in word final position). ... Stress in Asheninca follows a left-to-right iambic pattern – where feet can be (LL), (LH), or (H) – as illustrated by the fact that stress falls on all heavy syllables (as in 32b) and on even-numbered syllables in a string of light syllables (32a). Final syllables are considered to be extrametrical and are never stressed, even if the final syllable is heavy (e.g., [jíñaa] ‘water’, *[jiñáa]). sweep_summary: Two works with stress in the title. (1) Pater 2000 (Phonology) is about English secondary stress; Glottolog's own record shows it was attached to pich1237 by a 'computerized assignment from "ranked"', and the Cambridge abstract names no language but English: irrelevant, priority none. The real gain: the English original, Payne 1990 'Asheninca stress patterns' (the catalog's unheld primary; DOI paywalled, archive.org scan lending-restricted), was read first-hand at snippet level through the Internet Archive full-text-search highlight API with an identifier filter, yielding 194 verbatim scanned fragments (saved). They give the core statements directly: alternating stress from the second syllable, final syllable never stressed (extrametrical) except three lexically stressed suffixes, Heavy (branching-nucleus) syllables always stressed unless word-final, primary stress on the rightmost stressed syllable unless a heavier syllable outranks it, four-grade weight scale Heavy/Normal/Light/Extra-light, rapid-speech deletions, and fn.1 fixing the variety as Pichis. This confirms the catalog's weight-hedged coding and supersedes the second-hand McGarrity 2003/Rasin 2017 quotations as the deciding quote, though only as fragments; the full chapter (or the 1991 Spanish version) is still worth acquiring (high) for the complete rule (32) conditions and example sets. The held J. Payne 1989 Lecciones pp.34-43 was re-read and matches the 1990 fragments point for point.

new_statements.reading: Pichis Ashéninka has weight-sensitive, left-to-right alternating (iambic) stress: stress starts on the second syllable and hits every second syllable, the final syllable is extrametrical and never stressed (save three lexically stressed word-final suffixes), Heavy syllables (branching nucleus: long vowel or diphthong) are always stressed unless word-final and restart the count, and primary stress goes to the rightmost stressed syllable unless a heavier syllable in the relevant window outranks it (nucleus a counts as heavier than e/o/i; a Normal penult beats a stressed Light final). Syllable weight is a four-grade scale Heavy > Normal > Light (Ci) > Extra-light (tsi/shi-type, which reject stress), with rapid-speech deletion of Light-syllable stresses. This is exactly the system the catalog codes as weight-hedged with CVV heavy, final extrametrical and right-edge primary; it confirms the classification and adds the four-grade scale, the nucleus-quality tie-break and the three-suffix exception.

new_statements.quote: En las palabras formadas por sílabas normales, el patrón de acentuación empieza en la segunda sílaba y se acentúan todas las sílabas pares a la derecha, pero no la última sílaba de la palabra [...] Todas las sílabas fuertes son acentuadas, salvo cuando están al final de la palabra, sin importar el patrón de acentuación de la palabra. [...] El acento primario recae sobre la última sílaba fuerte que puede ser la penúltima, la antepenúltima y la antes de la antepenúltima sílaba. Después del acento primario, no hay acento secundario. [...] Si ninguna de las cuatro últimas sílabas es fuerte, el acento primario recae en la última sílaba que lleva acento.
new_statements.translation: In words made up of normal syllables, the stress pattern begins on the second syllable and all even-numbered syllables to the right are stressed, but not the last syllable of the word [...] All strong syllables are stressed, except when they are at the end of the word, regardless of the word's stress pattern. [...] Primary stress falls on the last strong syllable, which may be the penultimate, the antepenultimate or the one before the antepenultimate. After the primary stress there is no secondary stress. [...] If none of the last four syllables is strong, primary stress falls on the last syllable that carries stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the existing statement from Payne 1990 (weight-sensitive, left-to-right alternating from the 2nd syllable, final syllable never stressed, heavy CVV syllables always stressed unless final and restarting the count, primary stress at the right edge, four-grade weight scale, three lexically stressed final suffixes). The 1989 pedagogical grammar adds: the primary-stress rule stated as 'last strong syllable within the final four syllables, else last stressed syllable' with the weak/normal exception; the two-syllable-word rule (initial stress except dead-initial + voiceless onset); the speech-rate conditioning of weak-syllable stress; and names the lexically stressed final suffixes…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Four-grade syllable strength: fuerte (long vowel or diphthong), normal (a, e, o, or i before tautosyllabic n/m), débil (i not before n/m), muerta (shi, tsi). Default pattern: stress the 2nd syllable and every even syllable rightwards, never the final syllable (left-to-right iambic alternation with final extrametricality). Strong syllables are always stressed (unless word-final) and restart the even-syllable count after them; a preceding stressed normal syllable may optionally lose its stress and a preceding stressed weak syllable does lose it. Weak syllables take pattern stress only under conditions of word length, the following syllable's strength (a following a-syllable demotes them to dead in 4-syllable words) and speech rate (stressed in slow careful speech, unstressed in rapid speech); dead syllables never take stress (the stress shifts to an adjacent non-final syllable or is dropped). Two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable, except dead-initial words whose second syllable begins with a voiceless/aspirated consonant, which stress the second. Primary stress: the last strong syllable among the penult, antepenult and pre-antepenult; otherwise the last stressed syllable, except that if that last stressed syllable is weak and the preceding stressed syllable is normal, the normal syllable takes primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words have multiple stresses ('acento múltiple'); one is primary (greater intensity), the others secondary; explicitly 'Después del acento primario, no hay acento secundario' (no secondary stress after the primary), p. 42.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-syllable stress in vocatives, imperatives, and words carrying the distal demonstrative suffix -ntó and the exclamative suffix -vé, which 'llevan su propio acento o énfasis' and make the word not follow the Lección 2 rules (p. 62); -vé 'siempre está al final de la palabra y siempre es acentuado' (p. 149). Dead syllables (shi, tsi) never stressed; final syllable never stressed by the pattern; two-syllable words initial-stressed with the dead-initial + voiceless-onset exception; speech-rate variation for weak syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Payne 1989 (SLP 28) states in its introduction (p. 14) that it treats 'principalmente de la variedad ashéninca del Pichis' with notes on Alto Perené, and lists four regional varieties (Pichis, Alto Perené, Ucayali, Apurucayali); the stress rules are given for the Pichis variety, matching glottocode pich1237. Payne 1991 is catalogued by SIL under Pichis Ashéninka [cpu].
